cap.n0: Ask a model to finish "My dog loves" twice.|You can get two different answers.
cap.n1: That is not a glitch. It is a dial.
cap.n2: Tonight,|from Professor Yufei Ding's CSE 291P at UC San Diego:|how a model picks its next word,|and the two knobs that steer it.
cap.n3: Last episode's clerk is back.|Feed in "My dog loves", 3 tokens,|and out come about 200,000 scores, one per dictionary entry.
cap.n4: Each score is called a logit.|So which drawer does he open?
cap.n5: First, a function called softmax turns the scores|into odds that add up to 100 percent.
cap.n6: Here are made-up odds for our dog.|Walks, 45 percent. Treats, 30.|Naps, 12. Sticks, 8. Baths, 4.
cap.n8: Picking a word from these odds is called decoding.|The simplest way: take the top word, every time.|That's greedy.
cap.n9: On paper, greedy says walks, every time.|Our two answers need something else.
cap.n10: Her slide 28 runs greedy on a little tree of words,|starting from "The".
cap.c2: For example, this one we will choose nice,|and then we will choose woman, like the nice woman.
cap.n11: A sentence's odds are its words' odds, multiplied.|0.5 times 0.4: the nice woman scores 0.2.
cap.n12: But follow dog: next comes has, at 0.9.|The best word can hide behind a weaker one.
cap.n13: Beam search keeps the best two paths at every fork:|two hikers, two lanterns.
cap.n14: On her slide, it finds "the dog has":|0.4 times 0.9 is 0.36, beating 0.2.
cap.n15: Better, but still no guarantee. And it has a habit.
cap.c4: But later on, beam search has an issue.|The issue is, usually beam search people find that|they are preferring short sentence.
cap.n16: Every extra word multiplies in another number below one,|so longer sentences score lower.|Left alone, beam search drifts short.
cap.n17: Greedy and beam both chase the likeliest words,|and the text comes out bland, and loops.|People don't write that way.
cap.n18: So let chance in.|Sampling rolls a weighted die: on our odds,|walks comes up 45 times in 100, treats 30.
cap.n19: That's our puzzle, solved.|Left alone, the temperature setting,|a dial for how random the draw is,|sits at 1: every reply is a fresh draw.
cap.n20: Walks one time, treats the next.
cap.n21: And about once in 100 draws, the dog loves homework.
cap.n22: Sample from everything,|and now and then a silly word gets through.
cap.n23: One fix is top-k:|keep only the k likeliest words, then roll.|Her slide's picture uses k equals 6.
cap.c6: if you use the top six,|the overall accumulated probability of the top six tokens|only adding up to 0.68.
cap.n24: That was the word after "The": a flat step.|Now the word after "The car": a sharp one.
cap.c7: But for this one, if you have top six,|you already covered 99% of the overall probability.
cap.n25: A fixed k is too small when many words are fine,|and too big when only a few are.
cap.n26: Top-p lets the group size itself.|Line the words up, add their odds until you reach p,|keep that group, and draw from it.
cap.n27: With p at 0.92, her slide keeps 9 words in the flat step,|and only 3 in the sharp one.
cap.n28: Back to the dog, with p at 0.9.|Walks, treats, naps, sticks: together, 95 percent.|Baths and homework are out.
cap.n29: So which p should you try?
cap.c10: You should always try 0.9 at the beginning.
cap.n30: That's her starting point.|The paper behind top-p used 0.95.|The API's default is 1, which cuts nothing.
cap.n31: The second knob reshapes the odds before anything is cut:|temperature.
cap.n32: Her slide 32 puts it in one line:|divide every score by T, then softmax.
cap.n33: Below 1, the favourite pulls ahead.|Above 1, the odds even out.
cap.n34: Here's the dial. It goes from 0 to 2, and starts at 1.
cap.n35: Turn it down to 0.2. Walks jumps to 88 percent.
cap.n36: Turn it toward 0, and you are back to greedy.
cap.n37: One honest limit. Even at temperature 0,|one 2025 test got 80 different answers in 1,000 runs.|A busy server batches many requests together,|and the batch size changes the arithmetic.
cap.c9: But after you divide it by the temperature,|they are kind of similar.|So that's why when you have high temperature,|you will see like it's pretty flat.
cap.n39: Homework goes from 1 in 100 to about 1 in 20.
cap.n40: That's the high-temperature dog.|Add top-p at 0.9, and the cut still stops before homework.
cap.n41: So where should the dial sit?|Her slide 34 gives a rule of thumb.
cap.n42: Code: 0 to 0.2. Chat: about 0.7. Stories: 0.8 to 1.2.
cap.n43: Her slides pair the two knobs, and so did our dog.|The API's own reference says:|change temperature or top_p, generally not both.
cap.n44: Low for code: you want the same, careful answer.|In a story, a dog that loves homework might be the point.
cap.n45: The API has other knobs too:|max output tokens, two penalties, and a seed.
cap.n46: A seed asks for a repeatable draw:|best effort, not a guarantee.
cap.n47: Sometimes you want different answers, on purpose.
cap.n48: Sample several reasoning paths,|answers worked out step by step,|and they don't always agree. Her toy example:
cap.c11: For example, 1 plus 1,|some passes will give you the result 2,|some passes will give you the result 3.
cap.n49: So count, and go with the answer most paths reach.|That's self-consistency, from Wang and colleagues, 2022.
cap.n50: The catch: 5 paths cost about 5 answers' worth of tokens.
cap.n51: Back to our two answers.|Not a glitch: the dial sat at 1,|and the model rolled the die twice.
cap.n52: Turn it down for careful code, up for stories.|And if the dog ever loves homework, now you know why.
